transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello doctor, I'm Antonio. Lately, I've been feeling really scattered and overwhelmed because I keep forgetting everyday things like appointments and errands. It’s starting to really mess up taking care of my wife and my commitments in the community garden project.
Can you tell me more about these memory problems, have you also noticed any difficulty with learning new information or following instructions?

Yes, I really struggle with following through on things; I'll start sorting my wife's medication or writing a story for the kids, but get distracted halfway through and wander off to the garden. I also completely forget daily tasks, like intending to call her physiotherapist or pick up a prescription, and only realize hours later when my wife asks me about it.

Antonio, aside from feeling scattered and overwhelmed, have you noticed any changes in your mood, such as feeling sad, empty, or hopeless, or perhaps a lack of interest in activities you usually enjoy?
No, I haven't really felt sad, empty, or hopeless at all. I still have a lot of interest in my gardening and storytelling, though I find it really hard to stay focused enough to actually finish them.
Antonio, do you experience any excessive worry or anxiety about your forgetfulness or the tasks you're having trouble completing?

I definitely feel very stressed, frustrated, and overwhelmed by the mistakes I've been making lately. However, I'm not really sure if I would call it excessive worry or clinical anxiety; it's more just a deep frustration with myself.

Can you tell me more about this frustration with yourself, is it primarily related to your memory issues and inability to complete tasks, or are there other aspects of your life where you feel similarly frustrated?

Yes, the frustration is entirely about my memory slips and failing to finish things, especially because of how it impacts my wife and my community projects. I feel terribly guilty that she can't rely on me for her appointments or insurance paperwork, and I've even had to pull back from the garden and storytelling because I keep letting people down. It's really just about not being able to follow through on my responsibilities.
Antonio, can you describe if there are any specific times or situations when your memory problems and feelings of frustration seem to worsen or improve?

My frustration really peaks when I'm forced to sit still and focus on detailed tasks like filling out insurance forms or waiting in clinic lines, where any little distraction like a bird outside completely derails me. On the other hand, I feel much better when my days are loosely structured and I can freely bounce between active hobbies like gardening, cooking, and painting without the pressure of paperwork or schedules.

Antonio, when you're engaged in these active hobbies like gardening or painting, do you find that you're able to focus and see them through to completion without getting distracted, or do you still struggle with finishing what you start?

Even with the hobbies I love, like painting or gardening, I really struggle to stay focused and actually finish them. When I'm painting, I get very antsy, talk to myself, and keep getting up to do other things. With gardening or writing stories, I often wander off halfway through to do something else, leaving them incomplete.
Antonio, do you often act on impulse, doing things without much consideration for the consequences, such as interrupting others, blurting out answers, or intruding on conversations?

Yes, I definitely struggle with that, especially when it comes to interrupting and blurting out answers. During garden committee meetings or medical appointments, I often jump in with what I think someone is about to say before they can even finish. It's only afterward that I realize I've cut them off or missed an important detail they were trying to share.
Can you think of any situations where you've acted on impulse without considering the consequences, such as spending money, driving recklessly, or engaging in risky behaviors?

No, I haven't really struggled with those kinds of risky behaviors like reckless driving or impulsive spending. My impulsiveness is mostly just jumping into conversations too quickly or getting impatient when I have to wait in lines.
Do you often feel restless or fidgety, especially in situations where you're required to sit still for a long time, like in meetings or during meals?

Absolutely, I get this jumpy energy in my body whenever I have to sit still, like in clinic waiting rooms or when sitting with my wife. I constantly shift in my seat and look for any excuse to stand up. Even when I'm trying to relax with my hobbies, I get so antsy that I can't just sit there quietly.

Have you experienced difficulties with organization and time management, such as struggling to keep track of assignments or tasks, or frequently losing things, in addition to your memory problems and impulsivity?

Yes, my organization is a total mess, and I am constantly losing things like my glasses, the notebook with my appointment times, or important insurance folders. I really struggle to keep track of daily schedules, and even when I start a task like sorting my wife's medication, I'll get sidetracked and wander off halfway through.
Antonio, have you experienced an increase in physical activity or a tendency to engage in excessive running, climbing, or other physical activities, especially as a child or during periods of stress?

Yes, back in primary school, my teachers always complained that I couldn't sit still and was constantly on the move. At 65, I'm obviously not running or climbing on things, but I feel a constant inner restlessness and am always on the go, bouncing between chores and hobbies. My daughter even jokes that I never stop moving, though I still struggle to actually finish anything.

Antonio, can you tell me at what age you first started noticing these symptoms of inattention, impulsivity, and restlessness, and have they been present throughout your life or did they start more recently?

These tendencies are actually lifelong, tracing back to primary school where my teachers always complained that I couldn't sit still, constantly talked out of turn, and left my worksheets unfinished. While these traits were manageable during my loosely structured retirement, they became a major, overwhelming problem about 14 months ago when I had to take on my wife's care and paperwork after her stroke.

You mentioned that these symptoms have been present since primary school, but they became more problematic about 14 months ago; can you clarify if there was a specific change or event around that time that made your symptoms more noticeable or problematic?

Yes, about 14 months ago, my wife suffered a minor stroke, which changed everything because I suddenly had to take on a massive load of new responsibilities. I had to start managing her medical appointments, sorting her medications, and handling complex insurance paperwork on top of my usual community projects. This sudden demand for strict organization and scheduling is what completely exposed my lifelong attention difficulties and made them so problematic.

Have you experienced any significant decline in your cognitive function or memory over the past 14 months, or have your difficulties primarily been related to attention, impulsivity, and restlessness since childhood?

No, it is definitely not a new cognitive decline. These issues with attention, restlessness, and finishing tasks are the exact same patterns I've had since childhood, when my primary school teachers complained I couldn't sit still or finish my worksheets. The past 14 months of caregiving just piled on so much structure and stress that my lifelong difficulties finally caught up with me.

You've mentioned that these symptoms have been present since childhood, but became more problematic 14 months ago with increased responsibilities; can you confirm if you experienced any significant symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity prior to the age of 12?

Yes, these difficulties definitely date back to my childhood. Even in primary school, my teachers were always telling my parents that I couldn't sit still and was constantly talking out of turn. I'd also leave half-finished worksheets on my desk because I'd completely lose track of what we were supposed to be doing.
